Title: ChemBERTa-Informed Matrix Linear Models Improve Metabolomic Association Estimation
Abstract: Metabolomics studies measure hundreds of correlated molecules, but conventional analyses typically estimate each metabolite separately, producing noisy biomarker–metabolite associations. We investigated whether ChemBERTa-derived molecular representations could provide biologically meaningful structure to a matrix linear model and improve estimation. Data from 784 participants included eight clinical variables and 535 metabolites across eight biological pathways. Chemical SMILES strings were encoded into 384 ChemBERTa features, and distances between these representations were used to construct molecular similarity kernels. ChemBERTa distances preserved meaningful chemical organization, demonstrating concordance with lipid composition based on total double bonds (Mantel Spearman ρ = 0.608). For metabolite prediction, ordinary metabolite-wise regression provided the apparent performance ceiling (mean R² = 0.0344; mean squared error [MSE] = 0.009724), while increasingly restrictive molecular representations reduced predictive performance. However, ChemBERTa-informed subspaces improved estimation of biomarker–metabolite associations relative to rank-matched random subspaces across most balanced data splits, and the distance-based kernel outperformed features derived from principal-component analysis. These findings indicate that ChemBERTa features preserve relevant chemical relationships and can stabilize estimates of biomarker–metabolite effects, supporting their use as prior structure for biomarker discovery and mechanistic interpretation.
